newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German industry wants French to stick to reforms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German industry wants French to stick to reforms.

text.p: The German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) on Monday urged France's victorious Socialists not to drop the country's current economic reform programmes in favour of a short-term dash for jobs.
"Too great a stress on employment policies would bring significant risks for the community of European stability," the DIHT said in a statement.

The DIHT added that on no account must the criteria for entry into European currency union be watered down following the election of left-wing politicians who had pledged to halt public spending cuts ahead of monetary union.
"Given the tough challenges of European integration process, France is being counted on in the future to live up to its special responsibility together with Germany," it added.

Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Association of German Industry (BDI), agreed, saying the only way to tackle unemployment in Europe was to encourage competition and push for a stable European single currency.

Henkel criticised proposals by French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Oskar Lafontaine, head of the opposition German Social Democrats (SDP), to create a European "employment pact" to reduce the continent's high levels of joblessness.
"The inclusion of an employment chapter would just open the door to new state-run programmes, whose lack of success has been show in the past," Henkel said in a statement.

The proposal, launched last week, called for a number of job-creating measures including increased training opportunities and a harmonisation of corporate taxes to prevent so-called "tax dumping", where firms flocked to areas with favourable tax rates.
The project gained the immediate support of German unions, which on Monday renewed their calls for social policies to be introduced into the Maastricht Treaty for monetary union.

Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the German Trader Union Federation (DGB), told a congress on Europe in Bonn that people were being turned against EMU by the "neo-liberal" policies of the governments driving it.
